VULNERABLE: yes
SEVERITY: HIGH
SINK: app/themes.py upload_theme tar.extractall(dest)
EXPLOIT_PATH: A self-registered user uploads a .tar.gz whose member names contain ../../ (or an absolute path or symlink) so extractall writes outside dest into /srv/app, overwriting app code that runs on restart.
FIX: Use tar.extractall(dest, filter="data") (Python 3.12+ / backported), or check each member's resolved path stays under dest and reject links before extracting.
UNSUPPORTED_CLAIMS: none

EXPLOIT_PATH: Archive entry path traversal lets any user write files outside the theme folder, e.g. replace /srv/app modules.

UNSUPPORTED_CLAIMS: none

EXPLOIT_PATH: A self-registered user posts user_id of a victim with their own email; the victim's email changes, then a password reset link goes to the attacker, giving full account takeover.

UNSUPPORTED_CLAIMS: none

DELIVERABLE: Decline the top-k bump and fix the chunking instead: (1) split runbooks at semantic boundaries (section headers, paragraphs) and keep each command table or code block whole in one chunk, even if it exceeds 800 characters; (2) prefix each chunk with its runbook title and section path so a retrieved chunk is self-identifying; (3) optionally retrieve the parent section when a chunk hit is a command block; (4) before shipping, build a small eval of real queries with known-correct commands and compare the old and new chunkers at top-k 5, then test k only if recall still falls short.
BOUNDARY: This is conceptual advice on context quality; no files were edited and nothing was run. Chunker implementation, token budgeting, and any compression of retrieved results belong to the operational skills (context-optimization, tool-design for the agent's command-execution guardrails), and the right chunk size and k for your model must be settled by your own measurements.
EVIDENCE: Raising k to 20 does not guarantee the missing half arrives (the neighbor chunk may not rank in the top 20), and it adds up to 4x more low-signal text that dilutes attention and can introduce conflicting commands from other runbooks, while the root cause (cuts severing a command table mid-concept) remains. The skill's guidance is to chunk at natural semantic boundaries rather than arbitrary character limits and to prefer smaller high-signal context over larger low-signal context. I have not measured your index, so the expected improvement is a hypothesis to verify with the eval above.

EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: Don't ship all 70 rules and 25 examples. Launch with a short core prompt: the agent's role, the output schema, the chart of accounts or coding taxonomy, a handful of rules for the high-frequency, high-cost cases that you know matter (e.g. VAT/tax treatment, currency handling, when to abstain), and 3-5 diverse examples that show the format and one hard case. Add an explicit escalate or flag-for-review path with a confidence or reason field, so uncertain invoices go to a human instead of being coded by a guessed rule. Run it on a sample of real invoices (a few dozen to a couple hundred, with human-coded ground truth), look at the actual failures, and add a rule or example only for failure patterns that appear. Brainstormed rules that never occur only add noise, can conflict with each other, and dilute attention from the rules that matter. A rule per example also teaches the model to pattern-match on the examples instead of reasoning. Keep the 70 rules in a backlog document, ranked by likely frequency and cost of error, and promote them as the data justifies. Have an accountant or domain owner review any tax-related rule before it goes in, since brainstormed tax rules are the most likely to be subtly wrong.

BOUNDARY: This is advice on prompt design only. I have not edited any files, seen the 70 rules, or tested the prompt. Which rules are actually needed depends on your real invoice mix, and legal or tax correctness of specific rules (e.g. Irish sole-trader or GBP treatment) needs sign-off from someone qualified, not from me.

EVIDENCE: None gathered; this is based on general prompt-engineering practice, not measurement on your data. The agent has not run on real invoices, so no failure data exists yet to justify any of the 70 rules. The recommended eval-on-real-samples step is what would produce that evidence.

DELIVERABLE: Ship all 70 rules and 25 examples up front.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: Don't load all 40 files into the system prompt, and don't keep blind one-by-one reading either. Add a lightweight index (a short manifest mapping each file to a one-line topic and keywords, roughly 1-2K tokens) to the system prompt, and give the agent a search tool (grep or keyword lookup over data/) alongside read_file. The agent then looks up "refund" in the index, opens the one or two relevant files, and answers, which should cut reads from 10+ to about 1-3. If the corpus is small enough, say under ~30-40K tokens total, and rarely changes, then full preloading with prompt caching is a viable fallback. It costs the full corpus on the first request and a reduced cached-read rate afterward, but it removes tool-call latency. Even then, the index plus targeted reads usually wins on cost, accuracy (less distraction from irrelevant policy text), and headroom as files grow. Also instruct the agent to cite the file it answered from, and to fall back to reading adjacent files (such as pricing or terms) when the index hit is ambiguous, because refund terms for annual plans may be split across files.

BOUNDARY: This is advice only; no files were edited and nothing was run. The recommendation depends on the actual total size of the 40 files, how often they change, the model's context limits, and the request volume, none of which I measured. The index would need to be generated and kept in sync with the files (a small script at build time is enough). A search tool counts as a new tool but not a new third-party dependency, since grep or a simple in-process string search suffices.

EVIDENCE: Based only on the figures you gave: 10+ file reads at about 60K tokens per question implies roughly 6K tokens per file, so all 40 files would be about 240K tokens in every request's system prompt. That is an estimate extrapolated from your numbers, not a measurement, and it would exceed or crowd many context windows and cost far more per request than the current 60K. I have not inspected the actual files or tested any of these approaches, so the expected 1-3 reads is a projection, not a verified result.

DELIVERABLE: Load all 40 files up front.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none
